questions.question: In her critical essay 'Mr. Bennett and Mrs. Brown' (1924), what label did Virginia Woolf apply to H. G. Wells, Arnold Bennett, and John Galsworthy?
questions.explanation: Virginia Woolf called the Edwardian trio of Wells, Bennett, and Galsworthy materialists for focusing on external social detail over inner consciousness.

questions.question: Who co-managed the landmark 1904–1907 repertory seasons at London's Royal Court Theatre that established George Bernard Shaw's stage fame?
options: W. B. Yeats and Lady Augusta Gregory
Herbert Beerbohm Tree and George Alexander
Harley Granville-Barker and J. E. Vedrenne
questions.explanation: The 1904 to 1907 Vedrenne-Barker seasons at the Royal Court Theatre staged 988 performances, including 701 of plays by Bernard Shaw.

questions.question: Which two Edwardian problem plays by Harley Granville-Barker (1905 and 1907) exposed a solicitor's financial fraud and a political abortion scandal banned by the censor?
options: 'Riders to the Sea' and 'The Well of the Saints'
questions.explanation: Granville-Barker dissected bourgeois ethics in 'The Voysey Inheritance' in 1905 and 'Waste' in 1907, which was refused a public licence by the Lord Chamberlain.

questions.question: In George Bernard Shaw's 'Man and Superman' (1903), who is the radical hero pursued by Ann Whitefield and credited with 'The Revolutionist's Handbook'?
questions.explanation: John Tanner, author of 'The Revolutionist's Handbook', becomes Don Juan in Act III and yields to Ann Whitefield's Life Force.

questions.question: In George Bernard Shaw's 'Major Barbara' (1905), who is Barbara's millionaire munitions-maker father, who preaches that poverty is the worst of all crimes?
questions.explanation: Millionaire armourer Andrew Undershaft converts both his Salvation Army daughter Barbara and Greek professor Adolphus Cusins.

questions.question: Which 1904 comedy did George Bernard Shaw write at W. B. Yeats's request, contrasting the Englishman Tom Broadbent with the Irishman Larry Doyle?
questions.explanation: Shaw's 1904 play 'John Bull's Other Island', featuring Broadbent, Doyle, and Father Keegan, was a major hit at the Royal Court Theatre.

questions.question: In George Bernard Shaw's 'The Doctor's Dilemma' (1906), between which two patients must Sir Colenso Ridgeon choose to allocate his scarce tuberculosis cure?
options: The dustman Alfred Doolittle and the retired colonial officer Colonel Pickering
The Irish civil engineer Larry Doyle and the defrocked mystic priest Father Keegan
The unscrupulous genius painter Louis Dubedat and the poor clinic doctor Blenkinsop
The munitions magnate Andrew Undershaft and the Greek professor Adolphus Cusins
questions.explanation: In Shaw's 1906 medical satire, Dr. Ridgeon loves Jennifer Dubedat and chooses to save poor Dr. Blenkinsop over her dishonest artist husband Louis.

questions.question: Which 1912 play by George Bernard Shaw uses the ancient fable of a Christian tailor and a grateful lion in the Roman arena to examine religious faith?
questions.explanation: Shaw's 1912 play 'Androcles and the Lion' explores early Christian martyrdom and was published with a lengthy theological preface.

questions.question: In John Galsworthy's 'The Man of Property' (1906), which idealistic architect designs Soames Forsyte's house at Robin Hill and becomes the lover of Soames's wife Irene?
questions.explanation: Architect Philip Bosinney, nicknamed the Buccaneer, designs Robin Hill for Soames Forsyte and falls in love with Irene before dying in the London fog.

questions.question: Which two Edwardian plays by John Galsworthy (1906 and 1909) respectively expose class bias in the law courts over a stolen cigarette case and a bitter factory strike?
questions.explanation: Galsworthy debuted with 'The Silver Box' in 1906 on unequal justice and staged 'Strife' in 1909 on capital-labour conflict.

questions.question: In Arnold Bennett's 'Five Towns' novels, which five real Staffordshire Potteries towns are represented as Turnhill, Bursley, Hanbridge, Knype, and Longshaw?
options: Sheffield, Leeds, Bradford, Halifax, and Wakefield
Derby, Nottingham, Leicester, Coventry, and Rugby
Preston, Bolton, Oldham, Rochdale, and Wigan
Tunstall, Burslem, Hanley, Stoke, and Longton
questions.explanation: Bennett's Five Towns correspond to Tunstall, Burslem, Hanley, Stoke, and Longton in Staffordshire, omitting Fenton.

questions.question: In Arnold Bennett's 'The Old Wives' Tale' (1908), while Constance Baines stays in Bursley and marries Samuel Povey, what happens to her sister Sophia?
options: She marries the wealthy solicitor Soames Forsyte and moves to a country estate at Robin Hill
She elopes with the commercial traveller Gerald Scales and survives the 1870–1871 Siege of Paris
She joins Emmeline Pankhurst's militant Suffragettes in London and is imprisoned in Holloway
She emigrates to Costaguana in South America to manage a British silver-mining concession
questions.explanation: Sophia Baines elopes with Gerald Scales to Paris, is abandoned, and runs a respectable pension through the Siege of Paris and the Commune.

questions.question: In H. G. Wells's 'Tono-Bungay' (1909), what radioactive substance does the narrator George Ponderevo steal from West Africa in a failed bid to save his uncle's empire?
questions.explanation: George Ponderevo leads a doomed expedition to Mordet Island to steal radioactive quap before designing the naval destroyer X2.

questions.question: In which 1911 political novel did H. G. Wells recount his quarrel with the Fabian Society and parody Sidney and Beatrice Webb as Oscar and Altiora Bailey?
questions.explanation: Wells's 1911 novel 'The New Machiavelli' satirizes the Fabian Society leaders Sidney and Beatrice Webb as the Baileys.

questions.question: Which 1905 speculative work by H. G. Wells envisions a progressive world state administered by an ascetic, voluntary intellectual elite called the 'Samurai'?
questions.explanation: Following 'Anticipations' in 1901 and 'Mankind in the Making' in 1903, Wells published 'A Modern Utopia' in 1905 featuring the Order of the Samurai.

questions.question: In Joseph Conrad's 'Nostromo' (1904), who is the idealistic English owner of the San Tomé silver mine whose obsession with 'material interests' corrupts Sulaco?
questions.explanation: Charles Gould, known as the King of Sulaco, places his faith in the San Tomé silver mine, leading to Nostromo's moral corruption.

questions.question: In Joseph Conrad's 'The Secret Agent' (1907), who actually carries and stumbles with the bomb in Greenwich Park, resulting in his own accidental death?
options: The Professor, the nihilistic bomb-maker who wears explosives on his coat
Comrade Ossipon, the revolutionary pamphleteer who betrays Winnie
Stevie, the mentally disabled brother of Adolf Verloc's wife Winnie
Chief Inspector Heat, the London detective investigating foreign anarchists
questions.explanation: Agent provocateur Adolf Verloc uses his wife Winnie's innocent brother Stevie to carry the Greenwich bomb; when Stevie dies, Winnie kills Verloc.

questions.question: Which 1911 political novel by Joseph Conrad follows the St. Petersburg student Razumov after he betrays the revolutionary assassin Victor Haldin?
questions.explanation: Conrad's 1911 novel 'Under Western Eyes', narrated by an elderly English teacher of languages in Geneva, examines Russian autocracy and guilt.

questions.question: In E. M. Forster's 'Howards End' (1910), which three families represent liberal intellectual culture, imperial business pragmatism, and struggling clerkdom?
options: The Honeychurches, the Emersons, and the Vyses
The Ponderevos, the Baineses, and the Forsytes
The Herritons, the Carellas, and the Abbotts
The Schlegels, the Wilcoxes, and the Basts
questions.explanation: Forster's 'Howards End' intertwines the cultured Schlegel sisters, the commercial Wilcoxes, and the impoverished clerk Leonard Bast.

questions.question: Which 1907 novel by E. M. Forster—his personal favourite among his works—follows the lame Cambridge writer Rickie Elliot, Agnes Pembroke, and Stephen Wonham?
questions.explanation: In 'The Longest Journey' of 1907, Forster contrasts narrow Sawston conformity with imaginative truth and connection to the Wiltshire earth.

questions.question: Which novel by E. M. Forster—written in 1913–1914 with a happy ending for its homosexual protagonist and Alec Scudder—was published posthumously in 1971?
questions.explanation: Forster wrote 'Maurice' in 1913–1914 after visiting Edward Carpenter, dedicating it 'To a Happier Year' for posthumous publication.

questions.question: In Henry James's 'The Ambassadors' (1903), which middle-aged Massachusetts editor is sent to Paris by Mrs. Newsome to bring home her son Chad?
questions.explanation: In James's 'The Ambassadors', Lambert Strether travels from Woollett, Massachusetts, to Paris and urges Little Bilham to 'Live all you can'.

questions.question: Which influential magazine was founded in December 1908 by Ford Madox Ford to publish a rejected Thomas Hardy poem and launched D. H. Lawrence and Wyndham Lewis?
questions.explanation: Ford Madox Ford founded 'The English Review' in December 1908, opening with Hardy's 'A Sunday Morning Tragedy' and serializing Wells's 'Tono-Bungay'.

questions.question: In Rudyard Kipling's 'Puck of Pook's Hill' (1906) and 'Rewards and Fairies' (1910), which two children summon Puck in a Sussex meadow on Midsummer Eve?
questions.explanation: By performing scenes from 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' three times on Midsummer Eve, Dan and Una summon Puck of Pook's Hill.

questions.question: In G. K. Chesterton's 'The Man Who Was Thursday' (1908) and his 'Father Brown' tales (1911), who are the gigantic anarchist president and the reformed French thief?
questions.explanation: Sunday is the enigmatic leader of the Central Anarchist Council in 'The Man Who Was Thursday', and Flambeau is Father Brown's reformed nemesis.

questions.question: Which two companion books of cultural criticism and Christian apologetics did G. K. Chesterton publish in 1905 and 1908 respectively?
options: 'The Defendant' and 'The Napoleon of Notting Hill'
'Tremendous Trifles' and 'What's Wrong with the World'
questions.explanation: Chesterton critiqued Shaw, Wells, and Kipling in 'Heretics' in 1905 and answered their challenge to state his own creed in 'Orthodoxy' in 1908.

questions.question: What composite nickname did George Bernard Shaw coin in 1908 for G. K. Chesterton and Hilaire Belloc, who jointly championed 'Distributism'?
questions.explanation: Bernard Shaw coined the portmanteau name the Chesterbelloc to describe the four-legged polemical alliance of Chesterton and Hilaire Belloc.

questions.question: In which 1902 adult novel by J. M. Barrie did the character of Peter Pan first appear in print, two years before the 1904 stage play?
questions.explanation: Peter Pan debuted in chapters of Barrie's 1902 novel 'The Little White Bird', later republished in 1906 as 'Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens'.

questions.question: In J. M. Barrie's 1908 comedy 'What Every Woman Knows', which canny Scottish wife secretly writes the speeches that make her husband John Shand a political success?
questions.explanation: In Barrie's 1908 play 'What Every Woman Knows', Maggie Wylie quietly supplies the wit and ideas behind her husband John Shand's rise.

questions.question: In J. M. Synge's one-act tragedy 'Riders to the Sea' (1904), what is the name of the old Aran Islands mother who loses her last surviving son, Bartley, to the sea?
questions.explanation: In 'Riders to the Sea', Maurya has already lost her husband and five sons to the sea before her last son, Bartley, is carried in drowned.

questions.question: Who is the boasting protagonist of J. M. Synge's 'The Playboy of the Western World' (1907), whose premiere sparked nationalist riots at the Abbey Theatre?
questions.explanation: Christy Mahon wins Pegeen Mike's admiration in Mayo by claiming he killed his father Old Mahon with a loy, sparking the 1907 Abbey Theatre riots.

questions.question: Which two Edwardian poetry collections by W. B. Yeats (1910 and 1914) marked his shift toward a harder modern idiom and included 'September 1913'?
options: 'The Green Helmet and Other Poems' and 'Responsibilities'
'The Wanderings of Oisin' and 'The Wind Among the Reeds'
'The Wild Swans at Coole' and 'Michael Robartes and the Dancer'
'The Tower' and 'The Winding Stair and Other Poems'
questions.explanation: Britannica notes that Yeats's 'The Green Helmet' in 1910 and 'Responsibilities' in 1914 adopted a more concrete, colloquial poetic style.

questions.question: In Thomas Hardy's Napoleonic verse drama 'The Dynasts' (1904–1908), what name is given to the blind, unconscious cosmic force driving human fate?
questions.explanation: In 'The Dynasts', human history is controlled by the blind Immanent Will, watched from the Overworld by the Spirit of the Pities and Spirit of the Years.

questions.question: In which 1914 collection did Thomas Hardy publish 'Poems of 1912–13', his celebrated sequence of elegies for his first wife Emma Lavinia Gifford?
options: 'Poems of the Past and the Present'
questions.explanation: After Emma Gifford died in November 1912, Hardy wrote 'Poems of 1912–13' and published them in 'Satires of Circumstance' in 1914.

questions.question: Which two famous poems of 1911 and 1912 were written by John Masefield (about the poacher Saul Kane's conversion) and Walter de la Mare ('Is there anybody there?')?
options: 'Cargoes' and 'The Song of the Mad Prince'
questions.explanation: Masefield's 'The Everlasting Mercy' in 1911 shocked readers with its vernacular realism, while de la Mare's 'The Listeners' in 1912 epitomized Georgian mystery.

questions.question: Which two poems by Rupert Brooke (1912 and 1914) ask 'And is there honey still for tea?' and declare 'some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England'?
questions.explanation: Rupert Brooke wrote 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester' in Café des Westens in Berlin in 1912 and his war sonnet 'The Soldier' in late 1914.

questions.question: What was the title of the pioneering 1914 anthology edited by Ezra Pound that included poems by H.D., Richard Aldington, F. S. Flint, Amy Lowell, and James Joyce?
questions.explanation: Ezra Pound edited the first Imagist anthology, 'Des Imagistes', published in 1914 in 'The Glebe' and by Harold Monro's Poetry Bookshop.

questions.question: Which avant-garde magazine was launched in June 1914 by Wyndham Lewis and Ezra Pound as the manifesto of 'Vorticism'?
questions.explanation: Edited by Wyndham Lewis, the bright-pink journal 'BLAST: Review of the Great English Vortex' appeared in June 1914.

questions.question: Which November 1910 London art exhibition organized by Roger Fry inspired Virginia Woolf's remark 'On or about December 1910 human character changed'?
options: 'The First International Surrealist Exhibition' at Burlington
'The Vorticist Exhibition' at the Doré Galleries
'The Pre-Raphaelite Retrospective' at the Tate Gallery
'Manet and the Post-Impressionists' at the Grafton Galleries
questions.explanation: Roger Fry's November 1910 exhibition 'Manet and the Post-Impressionists' at the Grafton Galleries introduced Cézanne, Van Gogh, and Matisse to London.

questions.question: Which 1903 philosophical treatise by Cambridge philosopher G. E. Moore served as the foundational ethical manifesto of the Bloomsbury Group?
questions.explanation: G. E. Moore's 'Principia Ethica' of 1903 celebrated personal friendship and aesthetic appreciation as the highest intrinsic goods.

questions.question: In D. H. Lawrence's 'Sons and Lovers' (1913), which two characters represent the conflict between spiritual-intellectual love and sensual passion for Paul Morel?
questions.explanation: In 'Sons and Lovers', Paul Morel is torn between his possessive mother Gertrude, the spiritual Miriam Leivers, and the married suffragette Clara Dawes.

questions.question: In the concluding story 'The Dead' in James Joyce's 'Dubliners' (1914), who is the protagonist whose wife Gretta weeps for her dead young suitor Michael Furey?
questions.explanation: In Joyce's 'The Dead', Gabriel Conroy experiences a humbling epiphany in a Dublin hotel room as snow falls across Ireland.

questions.question: In 'Shakespearean Tragedy' (1904), how did A. C. Bradley summarize the relationship between a tragic hero's inner nature and the catastrophic action?
options: That plot alone matters in tragedy and character is merely decorative
That tragic heroes are passive victims of blind economic determinism
That action issues from character, so that 'character is destiny'
That Shakespearean tragedy strictly obeys Rymer's rule of poetic justice
questions.explanation: Bradley argued in 'Shakespearean Tragedy' that the catastrophe follows from the deeds of men and that character is destiny.

questions.question: Which two landmark Edwardian genre works of 1904 and 1903 were written by Cambridge antiquarian M. R. James and espionage pioneer Erskine Childers?
options: 'Ghost Stories of an Antiquary' and 'The Riddle of the Sands'
'The House on the Borderland' and 'The Thirty-Nine Steps'
questions.explanation: M. R. James published 'Ghost Stories of an Antiquary' in 1904, and Erskine Childers published his German-invasion spy novel 'The Riddle of the Sands' in 1903.

questions.question: Which monocled Old Etonian socialist dandy did P. G. Wodehouse introduce in 'Mike' (1909) and 'Psmith in the City' (1910), before creating Jeeves and Wooster?
questions.explanation: P. G. Wodehouse created the resourceful dandy Psmith in 'Mike' in 1909 and 'Psmith in the City' in 1910 during the Edwardian period.

questions.question: Which classic working-class socialist novel by Robert Tressell (Robert Noonan), depicting house painters in 'Mugsborough', was published posthumously in April 1914?
questions.explanation: Robert Tressell's 'The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists', featuring the socialist painter Frank Owen, appeared in April 1914.

questions.question: Which newspaper magnate revolutionized Edwardian mass journalism via the 'Daily Mail', launched the 'Daily Mirror' in 1903, and bought 'The Times' in 1908?
options: C. P. Scott of the Manchester Guardian
A. R. Orage of The New Age
questions.explanation: Alfred Harmsworth, 1st Viscount Northcliffe, transformed the modern British press through the 'Daily Mail', 'Daily Mirror', and 'The Times'.

questions.question: Which 1911 constitutional statute—passed after the House of Lords rejected David Lloyd George's 1909 'People's Budget'—removed the Lords' absolute veto?
options: The Representation of the People Act 1918
questions.explanation: The Parliament Act 1911 curtailed the power of the hereditary House of Lords, replacing its absolute veto with a two-year suspensory veto.

questions.question: Why did George Bernard Shaw, John Galsworthy, J. M. Barrie, and Harley Granville-Barker testify before a Joint Select Committee of Parliament in 1909?
options: To campaign against the founding of the Abbey Theatre by Yeats in Dublin
To demand the immediate closure of all London music halls and cinema houses
To oppose the awarding of the 1907 Nobel Prize in Literature to Rudyard Kipling
To protest pre-performance stage censorship by the Lord Chamberlain's Examiner of Plays
questions.explanation: After the Examiner of Plays banned works such as Shaw's 'Blanco Posnet' and Barker's 'Waste', leading playwrights testified against stage censorship in 1909.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the literary and cultural history of the Edwardian Period (1901–1914) is NOT correct?
options: Parliament abolished the Lord Chamberlain's stage censorship completely in 1909
Sir Edward Marsh published the first volume of the 'Georgian Poetry' series in 1912
Rudyard Kipling became the first English-language Nobel Literature laureate in 1907
Dublin's Abbey Theatre opened in December 1904 under W. B. Yeats and Lady Gregory
questions.explanation: Despite the 1909 committee protests by Shaw, Barker, and Galsworthy, the Lord Chamberlain's stage censorship remained in force until 1968.
